title: Snopek head injury went unnoticed, witness says; Second day of inquest into man's death in cells takes place in Cranbrook
article: A lack of communication appears to be a major factor in the tragic death of Ryan Glen Snopek.
On Tuesday, one of the key witnesses in the inquest into Snopek's death said he never knew about the head injury that ultimately killed the 30-year-old Cranbrook resident.

At about 10 a.m. on Jan. 1, 2006 a prison guard noticed that Snopek was having trouble breathing and notified on-duty officers. Snopek received cardio-pulmonary resuscitation and was rushed to East Kootenay Regional Hospital where he died at about 1:30 p.m.
Snopek was in cells after officers arrested him New Year's Eve for mischief and assault.
Ambulance attendant Edward Bannatyne provided evidence to the jury as to his assessment of the 30-year-old on Dec. 31, 2005.
According to Bannatyne, he and his partner were dispatched to an assault complaint. When they arrived in the carport area of 24-1500 2nd Street North, Snopek was in the back of a police cruiser.
Bannatyne said Snopek, who was cuffed, managed to walk over to the ambulance cot without being supported by a police officer.
"He sat down on the cot," Bannatyne said. "I asked him twice if he was hurt at all."
Bannatyne added, "He presented to me as being a very normal person at that point."
Both times Snopek said he wasn't hurt.
During his check, Bannatyne couldn't identify any deformities such as broken bones or bumps.
"I felt for his pulse -- it was a regular normal pulse," Bannatyne said. "He was breathing fine."
While conducting his assessment Bannatyne indicated he had no knowledge of either a head injury, neck injury or Snopek losing consciousness.

During the opening day of testimony, the court heard that Douglas McKendry had put Snopek in a headlock. During the hold, McKendry heard and felt a pop in Snopek's neck. When McKendry released Snopek, he stood up then fell backwards out a door onto a cement walkway. The back of Snopek's head hit the stoop and he momentarily lost consciousness.

Dr. William Currie, the pathologist who conducted the autopsy, determined the "good whack" to Snopek's skull caused a fracture, which in turn caused bleeding. The blood then slowly pooled around Snopek's brain.
"The pressure caused vital areas of the brain to short circuit," Currie testified.

In this case, the short circuiting impaired Snopek's breathing functions while in RCMP cells about 12 hours after his initial arrest. However, when Bannatyne arrived on scene the head injury information wasn't made available to him.
In retrospect, Bannatyne said his protocol would have been much different if he knew about the head injury.
Bannatyne said Snopek would have been placed on a backboard with a neck collar then transported to hospital.
The only suggestion that there might be more medical problems came from hearsay.

"As I was putting away the cot I overheard somebody say (Snopek) had been unconscious," Bannatyne said. "I walked over to the police car, where the female police officer was standing. I said, 'The patient needs to be watched.'"
In response, Bannatyne recalled the female officer said Snopek wasn't "going to hospital. He's going to jail."
Bannatyne said a male officer standing on the opposite side of the cruiser assured him there were guards on duty 24-hours a day.
"I didn't feel to be in control of the patient or the scene and left it at that," Bannatyne said.
However, Bannatyne emphasized nobody at scene -- neither emergency personnel or party goers -- directly told him about Snopek losing consciousness or the manner in which it happened.
"The only history I had was that Mr. Snopek was impaired, as relayed from the police officer," Bannatyne said.

Given the fact Bannatyne had done one assessment, police officers believed Snopek was cleared to go with them to cells. Both Constables Melody Henderson and Keeley Deley, who were the first emergency personnel on scene to deal with Snopek, testified they believed this to be the case.
"You didn't ask for a second evaluation," said Helen Roberts, who is a lawyer representing the RCMP.
"Correct," Bannatyne said.
"You weren't refused a second request for evaluation," Roberts said.
"Correct," Bannatyne said.
"You had no information regarding a head injury," said city solicitor Michael McAllister.
"Correct," Bannatyne said.
Given the police reassurance of 24-hour guards, Bannatyne told McAllister that "My expectation was that (Snopek) would be watched for a change in breathing or a loss of consciousness."
In fact, it was a guard who noticed Snopek's breathing difficulties while in cells the day he died.
However, through Henderson's evidence the court learned that guard's aren't allowed to go into cells to monitor patients without a police officer. Henderson explained this was for safety reasons.
The fact Bannatyne didn't conduct a second evaluation baffled lawyer Jesse Gelber, who represents the Snopek family.
"I don't get this," Gelber said.
Bannatyne conceded he could have re-evaluated Snopek "If I was more assertive at scene."
Gelber asked Bannatyne if he was intimidated by police.
Bannatyne replied, "No."
Bannatyne reiterated that he believed Snopek, "would be watched carefully."

Bannatyne's account differs from the evidence of McKendry, Brandy Zolynski and Gordon Van Benthien who testified to either warning dispatch, police or ambulance personnel about Snopek's head and potential neck injuries.
McKendry testified he told the 911 dispatcher about possibly breaking Snopek's neck and asking for ambulance personnel.

However, Roberts provided the 911 transcript to McKendry and noted there is no mention of a possible neck injury, that Snopek was unconscious or a specific request for ambulance personnel. Roberts noted the transcript indicates that McKendry reported a violent domestic situation.

A Coroner's inquest is a formal court proceeding held to publicly review the circumstances of a death and is mandatory when a death occurs in police custody. In all other cases, the decision to call an inquest is discretionary and is based on the particulars of the death.
A five-person jury -- in this case three women and two men -- are listening to evidence from witnesses under subpoena in order to determine the facts of the death.

Coroner Bruce Chamberlayne, who presides over this matter, is present to ensure the jury maintains the goal of fact finding, not fault finding -- which is different than in a criminal court case. However, the jury can make recommendations to prevent a similar death in the future or any other recommendation in connection with the death. These are included in a public document, the Verdict at Coroner's Inquest.
Only five witnesses remain to provide evidence.
